title: What Is Pharmacology?

items.text: ●  Pharmacology: the scientific study of how drugs interact with living systems — from the molecular level to the whole patient.
items.md: **●  Pharmacology:** the scientific study of how drugs interact with living systems — from the molecular level to the whole patient.

items.text: ●  Drug (medication): any chemical substance used to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent disease, or to alter a physiologic process.
items.md: **●  Drug (medication):** any chemical substance used to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent disease, or to alter a physiologic process.

items.text: ●  Pharmacologic effect: a measurable biological change a drug produces (e.g., lower blood pressure).
items.md: **●  Pharmacologic effect:** a measurable biological change a drug produces (e.g., lower blood pressure).

items.text: ●  Therapeutic effect: the intended, beneficial pharmacologic effect for a given condition.
items.md: **●  Therapeutic effect:** the intended, beneficial pharmacologic effect for a given condition.

items.text: ●  Adverse drug reaction (ADR): an unintended and harmful response occurring at normal therapeutic doses.
items.md: **●  Adverse drug reaction (ADR):** an unintended and harmful response occurring at normal therapeutic doses.

items.text: ●  Toxicity: harmful effects that occur as the dose or exposure exceeds the therapeutic range.
items.md: **●  Toxicity:** harmful effects that occur as the dose or exposure exceeds the therapeutic range.

notes: Emphasize that "therapeutic effect" and "pharmacologic effect" are not synonyms — a drug can have pharmacologic effects that are not therapeutic (that is often exactly what an adverse effect is).

title: Chemical, Generic, and Brand Names

items.text: ●  Generic name: the official, non-proprietary name assigned to the active drug — one generic name per drug, regardless of manufacturer.
items.md: **●  Generic name:** the official, non-proprietary name assigned to the active drug — one generic name per drug, regardless of manufacturer.

items.text: ●  Brand (trade) name: the manufacturer’s marketed name; the same generic drug may have several brand names, and brand names change between countries.
items.md: **●  Brand (trade) name:** the manufacturer’s marketed name; the same generic drug may have several brand names, and brand names change between countries.

title: Evidence-Based Drug Approval

items.text: ●  Efficacy: how well a drug works under ideal, controlled trial conditions.
items.md: **●  Efficacy:** how well a drug works under ideal, controlled trial conditions.

items.text: ●  Effectiveness: how well a drug works in everyday clinical practice, with real-world adherence and comorbidities.
items.md: **●  Effectiveness:** how well a drug works in everyday clinical practice, with real-world adherence and comorbidities.

items.text: ●  Benefit vs. risk: the central question regulators and prescribers must weigh for every approval and every prescription.
items.md: **●  Benefit vs. risk:** the central question regulators and prescribers must weigh for every approval and every prescription.

items.text: ●  Adverse-event reporting: ongoing, voluntary and mandatory reporting systems (e.g., FDA MedWatch) that catch safety signals after approval.
items.md: **●  Adverse-event reporting:** ongoing, voluntary and mandatory reporting systems (e.g., FDA MedWatch) that catch safety signals after approval.

notes: Efficacy vs. effectiveness is a favorite exam distinction — efficacy is the trial result, effectiveness is what happens once real patients with real adherence patterns use the drug.

title: Would You Prescribe It?

items.text: A new medication improves symptoms in 70% of patients with a chronic, non-life-threatening condition. In postmarketing data, it causes serious hepatotoxicity in about 1% of patients who take it.

items.text: Ask yourself:  Would you prescribe it — and does your answer depend on what else is available?

emphasis.text: Would you prescribe it — and does your answer depend on what else is available?

items.md: **Ask yourself:** **Would you prescribe it — and does your answer depend on what else is available?**

items.text: Clinical pearl:  Risk-benefit analysis is always comparative: a 1% serious-toxicity rate reads very differently if it is the only effective option versus if three safer alternatives already exist.

emphasis.text: Risk-benefit analysis is always comparative: a 1% serious-toxicity rate reads very differently if it is the only effective option versus if three safer alternatives already exist.

items.md: **Clinical pearl:** **Risk-benefit analysis is always comparative: a 1% serious-toxicity rate reads very differently if it is the only effective option versus if three safer alternatives already exist.**

notes: Good discussion question — push students to ask "compared to what?" rather than judging the number in isolation.

items.text: In which clinical trial phase is a drug first tested in a large patient population specifically to confirm efficacy and monitor for adverse effects at scale, just before approval?

emphasis.text: In which clinical trial phase is a drug first tested in a large patient population specifically to confirm efficacy and monitor for adverse effects at scale, just before approval?

items.md: **In which clinical trial phase is a drug first tested in a large patient population specifically to confirm efficacy and monitor for adverse effects at scale, just before approval?**

items.text: Why:  Phase III trials enroll hundreds to thousands of patients, often at multiple sites, to confirm efficacy and monitor safety at scale before approval. Phase I is small-scale safety/dosing, Phase II is preliminary efficacy, and Phase IV is postmarketing surveillance after approval.

title: Pharmacodynamics in One Pathway

items.text: ●  Drug target: the specific molecule a drug binds to produce its effect.
items.md: **●  Drug target:** the specific molecule a drug binds to produce its effect.

items.text: ●  Receptor: a protein target whose activation (or blockade) triggers a cellular response.
items.md: **●  Receptor:** a protein target whose activation (or blockade) triggers a cellular response.

items.text: ●  Signal transduction: the chain of molecular events that converts receptor binding into a cellular effect.
items.md: **●  Signal transduction:** the chain of molecular events that converts receptor binding into a cellular effect.

items.text: ●  Pharmacologic response: the measurable downstream result — contraction, secretion, gene transcription, and so on.
items.md: **●  Pharmacologic response:** the measurable downstream result — contraction, secretion, gene transcription, and so on.

notes: Write the chain on the board: drug -> target -> signal transduction -> response. Every pharmacodynamics topic for the rest of the course maps onto this chain somewhere.

title: Agonists vs. Antagonists

items.text: Partial agonist — submaximal activation, even at full receptor occupancy
items.md: Partial agonist — submaximal activation, even at full receptor occupancy

items.text: Inverse agonist — reduces baseline (constitutive) receptor activity

items.text: Competitive — reversibly competes with agonist at the same site; overcome by more agonist
items.md: Competitive — reversibly competes with agonist at the same site; overcome by more agonist

items.text: Noncompetitive — binds elsewhere or irreversibly reduces the maximal effect
items.md: Noncompetitive — binds elsewhere or irreversibly reduces the maximal effect

items.text: Irreversible — permanently inactivates the receptor until new receptor is synthesized
items.md: Irreversible — permanently inactivates the receptor until new receptor is synthesized

notes: A classic exam trap: a competitive antagonist shifts the dose-response curve right (same Emax, more drug needed); a noncompetitive/irreversible antagonist lowers the Emax instead.

title: The Therapeutic Index

items.text: Therapeutic Index (TI) = TD₅₀ ÷ ED₅₀ (toxic dose in 50% ÷ effective dose in 50%).

items.text: A wide TI means a large margin between an effective dose and a toxic dose — generally safer to dose.
items.md: A wide TI means a large margin between an effective dose and a toxic dose — generally safer to dose.

items.text: A narrow TI means effective and toxic doses are close together — requires careful dosing and often blood-level monitoring.

title: Routes of Administration
tables: Convenient; subject to first-pass metabolism and variable absorption
Absorbed directly into systemic circulation; bypasses first-pass metabolism
100% bioavailable; immediate onset; no absorption phase
Faster than oral; good for depot/long-acting formulations
Slower, steady absorption; common for insulin, heparin
Rapid local effect in the lungs; minimizes systemic exposure for some drugs
Slow, sustained systemic absorption through the skin
Local effect at the site of application; minimal systemic absorption
notes: Ask students which routes bypass first-pass metabolism (IV, sublingual, inhaled, transdermal, topical, SC, IM — essentially everything except oral).

title: Bioavailability

items.text: Bioavailability (F) = the fraction of an administered dose that reaches systemic circulation unchanged.

emphasis.text: Bioavailability (F) = the fraction of an administered dose that reaches systemic circulation unchanged.

items.md: **Bioavailability (F) = the fraction of an administered dose that reaches systemic circulation unchanged.**

items.text: By definition, an IV dose has 100% bioavailability — the entire dose enters the bloodstream directly.
items.md: By definition, an IV dose has 100% bioavailability — the entire dose enters the bloodstream directly.

items.text: Oral bioavailability is reduced by incomplete absorption and by first-pass hepatic metabolism.
items.md: Oral bioavailability is reduced by incomplete absorption and by first-pass hepatic metabolism.

notes: This naturally sets up the next slide on first-pass metabolism as the main reason oral bioavailability is less than 100%.

title: The First-Pass Effect

items.text: Examples with a large first-pass effect: nitroglycerin, propranolol, morphine — all require higher oral doses (or a non-oral route) to achieve the same systemic exposure as IV.

emphasis.text: Examples with a large first-pass effect: nitroglycerin, propranolol, morphine — all require higher oral doses (or a non-oral route) to achieve the same systemic exposure as IV.

items.md: **Examples with a large first-pass effect: nitroglycerin, propranolol, morphine — all require higher oral doses (or a non-oral route) to achieve the same systemic exposure as IV.**

notes: The liver can inactivate a large fraction of drug before it ever reaches systemic circulation — this is why some drugs are given sublingually or transdermally instead of orally.

title: Distribution

items.text: ●  Plasma protein binding: only unbound ("free") drug is pharmacologically active and able to cross membranes.
items.md: **●  Plasma protein binding:** only unbound ("free") drug is pharmacologically active and able to cross membranes.

items.text: ●  Lipid solubility: lipophilic drugs cross membranes more readily and distribute into fatty tissue.
items.md: **●  Lipid solubility:** lipophilic drugs cross membranes more readily and distribute into fatty tissue.

items.text: ●  Tissue perfusion: highly perfused organs (brain, heart, kidney) receive drug faster than poorly perfused tissue (fat, bone).
items.md: **●  Tissue perfusion:** highly perfused organs (brain, heart, kidney) receive drug faster than poorly perfused tissue (fat, bone).

items.text: ●  Volume of distribution (Vd): a calculated value relating total drug in the body to plasma concentration — a high Vd suggests extensive tissue distribution.
items.md: **●  Volume of distribution (Vd):** a calculated value relating total drug in the body to plasma concentration — a high Vd suggests extensive tissue distribution.

notes: Vd is a theoretical volume, not a real anatomic space — a drug with a very high Vd (like digoxin) is telling you it is mostly sequestered in tissue, not floating around in plasma.
